articleSummary:

- Malaria remains a global public health challenge, with about 600,000 deaths in 2024 per the World Health Organization, and Plasmodium falciparum causing roughly 90% of fatalities. Researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP), Faculdade de Ciências Farmacológicas (FCF-USP), identified 14 compounds derived from an anticancer drug that kill Plasmodium falciparum in vitro, affecting both asexual blood stages and gametocytes—the latter enabling transmission to mosquitoes. The study, published in ACS Omega and supported by FAPESP, suggests histone deacetylases as a promising therapeutic target, enabling rational design of more potent, selective molecules. articleSummary: As of 2026-09-16, a systematic review links rhabdomyolysis to SARS-CoV-2 infection and, rarely, to COVID-19 vaccination. articleHeadline: Doctors warn that RSV pneumonia is not just a disease of children; older adults are at risk of severe illness and may require hospitalization.
articleSummary: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia poses a serious risk in Thailand, especially for older adults: those over 75 and those aged 50–74 with comorbidities (lung, heart, diabetes, liver, kidney disease). Although often considered a pediatric illness, RSV can cause severe pneumonia requiring hospitalization or ICU care, with some cases needing mechanical ventilation. Mortality risk is markedly higher in the elderly, with individuals over 65 reportedly dying at about 10 times the rate of children aged 2–5. Early symptoms mimic a common cold, but can progress to dyspnea, pneumonia, wheeze, or heart failure exacerbation. There is no specific antiviral treatment; care is supportive. Vaccination is available in two types (adjuvanted and non-adjuvanted) and protects against both RSV A and B strains, recommended for high-risk groups. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, masks, distancing, and consulting a clinician for vaccination before infection, particularly ahead of the rainy season.

articleHeadline: Progress Against The World's Deadliest Infectious Diseases Is On A Knife-Edge
articleSummary: 2025 international funding cuts for HIV, TB and malaria disrupted programs, raising fears of reversing gains. HIV prevention was hardest hit, with PrEP users dropping from 1.4 million in 2024 to 1.1 million in 2025, and over 2 million adolescent girls and young women losing essential health services. TB programs experienced reduced community activities, contact investigation and active case finding, hindering early diagnosis and treatment; malaria programs faced stock-outs of medicines, setbacks in monitoring drug and insecticide resistance, and delays to prevention campaigns. Despite setbacks, programs adapted to extreme pressure: governments and health workers sustained lifesaving services, pursued efficiencies, and accelerated innovation. Notable positives include lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injectable PrEP, with first deliveries to Eswatini and Zambia in November 2025 and later rollout to eight more African countries; AI-driven TB screening in over 20 countries; near-point-of-care molecular diagnostics in 13 countries; and dual-ingredient nets showing potential to reduce malaria.

articleHeadline: FAQ: What you need to know about airport malaria in Frankfurt.
articleSummary: Two residents of Frankfurt’s Schwanheim district have malaria, likely from an imported Anopheles mosquito linked to the airport. They did not work at the airport nor recently travel to malaria-risk areas. In July, six airport employees were infected, two of whom died. Laboratory confirmation led to the health department notification. Airport malaria occurs when infected Anopheles mosquitoes from tropical regions reach Germany by plane or cargo and bite people; such cases are rare; the last Frankfurt airport case before this cluster was in 2023. Risk in Schwanheim is low; the cases are about five kilometers from the airport. Mosquitoes collected around the airport and the patients’ homes were sent to Antwerp Tropeninstituut for genetic analysis; no Anopheles mosquitoes have been found yet. Incubation is 7-15 days; transmission by local mosquitoes is theoretically possible but unlikely; climate change and higher flight traffic from Cameroon, Ghana, and Nigeria could increase future cases.
